subject: Vocabulary
description: Greek TELE (far, distant) and Latin DIST (apart, away) roots — telescope, telephone, telegraph, distance, distract, distinguish, distill.

questions.stem: TELE root means 'far'. TELESCOPE literally means a device for:

options.option_text: Seeing far (tele + scope=look)
Hearing distant sounds clearly
Communicating across distance
Walking great distances easily

questions.explanation: TELESCOPE — etymology TELE (far, Greek) + SKOPEIN (to look, see) = 'instrument for seeing far'. TELE WORD FAMILY (root TELE = far, distant): (1) TELEPHONE — 'far + sound' = sound from far. (2) TELEGRAPH — 'far + write' = writing from far. (3) TELEVISION — 'far + see' = seeing from far. (4) TELEPATHY — 'far + feeling' = communication of feelings from afar (mental). (5) TELESCOPE — 'far + look' = looking far. (6) TELEMETRY — 'far + measure' = measuring at distance. (7) TELECONFERENCE — meeting from far. (8) TELESCOPIC — relating to telescope; collapsible/extendable. SCOPE FAMILY (Greek 'skopein' = to look): MICROSCOPE (small + look), KALEIDOSCOPE (beautiful pattern + look), STETHOSCOPE (chest + look — heart auscultation), HOROSCOPE (hour + look — birth-time horoscope), GYROSCOPE (rotation + look), ENDOSCOPE (within + look — medical procedure), PERISCOPE (around + look — submarine), SPECTROSCOPE (spectrum + look). HISTORY: telescope invented by Hans Lippershey (1608, Netherlands); Galileo improved it (1609) — discovered Jupiter's moons, Saturn's rings, sunspots. Today: HUBBLE (1990), JAMES WEBB (2021) — most powerful space telescopes. PYQ FREQUENCY: TELE root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1-2× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Communication of thoughts across distance (mental)
Visual broadcast across great distances
Loud sound transmission to far areas
Distance measurement using sounds (sonar)

questions.explanation: TELEPATHY — etymology TELE (far) + PATHOS (feeling, suffering, Greek) = 'distant feeling/communication'. Generally refers to alleged direct mental communication between minds without using normal sensory channels. Historically debated as a paranormal phenomenon; rigorous scientific research has not confirmed reliable telepathic abilities. PATHOS WORD FAMILY: (1) PATHOLOGY — study of disease (-pathy = disease). (2) SYMPATHY — 'with + feeling' = sharing another's feelings (especially sorrow). (3) EMPATHY — 'in + feeling' = entering another's emotional state. (4) APATHY — 'without + feeling' = lack of interest or emotion. (5) ANTIPATHY — 'against + feeling' = strong dislike. (6) HOMEOPATHY — 'similar + suffering' = treatment based on 'like cures like'. (7) ALLOPATHY — 'other + suffering' = standard medical practice (using contrary causes). (8) PSYCHOPATHY — 'mind + suffering' = personality disorder. (9) NATUROPATHY — 'natural + therapy'. INDIA HEALTHCARE: AYUSH = AYURVEDA, YOGA, UNANI, SIDDHA, HOMEOPATHY — alternative medicine systems recognized; Ministry of AYUSH established 2014. TELEPATHY in pop-culture: Star Wars 'Force', X-Men's Professor X, etc. — fictional. Real WIRELESS BRAIN-TO-BRAIN communication research underway (Neuralink, BCIs). PYQ FREQUENCY: TELE-PATHY combo vocab in CAT, advanced English MCQs.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: DIST root means 'apart, away'. DISTRACT means to:

options.option_text: Pull attention away (dis + tract)
Make something denser packed
Bring closer together quickly
Obtain something in a hurry

questions.explanation: DISTRACT — etymology DIS (apart, away) + TRACT (pull, draw, from Latin 'trahere') = 'to pull away'. Means to DIVERT someone's ATTENTION. WORD FAMILY (root TRACT/TRAH = pull, draw): (1) ATTRACT (ad + tract) — pull TOWARDS. (2) DISTRACT (dis + tract) — pull APART/AWAY. (3) EXTRACT (ex + tract) — pull OUT. (4) SUBTRACT (sub + tract) — pull FROM UNDER. (5) CONTRACT (con + tract) — pull TOGETHER (also legal binding agreement). (6) DETRACT (de + tract) — pull DOWN, take away. (7) RETRACT (re + tract) — pull BACK. (8) TRACTOR — vehicle that PULLS. (9) TRACTION — pulling action. (10) PROTRACT — pull forward, prolong. (11) ABSTRACT (abs + tract) — pull away from, separate from concrete details. WORD FAMILY (DIS prefix = apart, away, not): DISTANCE, DISTINCT, DISTILL, DISCONTENT, DISTORT, DISTRESS, DISCOURAGE, DISADVANTAGE. KEY DISTINCTION: DIS = away/apart/not (Latin); DI = two (Greek, e.g., DIODE has 2 electrodes; DIOXIDE has 2 oxygens); DYS = bad (Greek, e.g., DYSFUNCTION, DYSLEXIA). PYQ FREQUENCY: TRACT root + DIS prefix vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 2-3 per paper.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Tell apart from others (recognize differences)
Erase something completely from view
Mix things together indistinctly
Hold tightly to a position firmly

questions.explanation: DISTINGUISH — etymology DIS (apart) + STINGUERE (Latin, to mark, prick) = 'to mark apart' = to RECOGNIZE DIFFERENCES; tell apart. SAMPLE USAGES: (1) 'Can you distinguish silk from polyester by touch?' (2) 'Twins are sometimes hard to distinguish.' (3) 'He distinguished himself in the field of mathematics' (= excelled, stood out). DOUBLE MEANINGS: 'distinguish' can mean (a) tell apart (most common), (b) become eminent, stand out (figurative). DISTINGUISHED — adjective: EMINENT, IMPORTANT, having achieved fame ('a distinguished scientist'). RELATED: (1) DISTINCT — clearly different, separate ('two distinct species'). (2) DISTINCTION — difference, eminence, honour ('graduated with distinction'). (3) INDISTINCT — vague, blurred. (4) EXTINGUISH (ex + stinguere) — put out, eradicate (a fire, a hope). (5) DISTINGUISHED-LOOKING — looking eminent, impressive. EXAM-FAVORITE distinction: DISTINGUISH (recognize difference) vs EXTINGUISH (put out a fire) — different prefixes, different meanings. SYNONYMS for distinguish: differentiate, discern, discriminate, identify. ANTONYMS: confuse, conflate, blend. PYQ FREQUENCY: DISTINGUISH-EXTINGUISH pair in SSC CGL synonyms-section, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Purify by evaporation and condensation
Mix substances together evenly
Dissolve a solid in water completely
Filter solid particles from liquid

questions.explanation: DISTILL — etymology DIS (apart) + STILLARE (drop, drip) = 'to drop down' (referring to liquid drops collected after vaporization). Process: liquid is HEATED → vapor rises → CONDENSES on cold surface → DRIPS DOWN as PURIFIED liquid. Used to: (1) PURIFY water (distilled water — extremely pure, used in lab/medical/automotive batteries). (2) Make ALCOHOLIC SPIRITS (whiskey, vodka, brandy — distilling fermented liquid increases alcohol concentration; etymology of 'spirit' = the rising essence). (3) Extract ESSENTIAL OILS from herbs/flowers (rose water, lavender oil, etc.). TYPES: (a) SIMPLE DISTILLATION — single stage; works if boiling points differ by > 25°C. (b) FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION — multiple stages with column; separates closer-boiling liquids (used in petroleum refining: gasoline, kerosene, diesel from crude oil). (c) STEAM DISTILLATION — for heat-sensitive volatiles. (d) VACUUM DISTILLATION — at reduced pressure. KEY EQUIPMENT: still, condenser, fractional column. METAPHORICAL USE: 'distill the essence of an idea' = extract the most important part. RELATED WORDS: DISTILLER, DISTILLATE, DISTILLERY. PYQ FREQUENCY: distillation in NEET, NCERT chemistry, SSC GA 1-2× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Perceive or recognize clearly
Refuse to acknowledge openly
Confuse and mix things up
Hide something out of sight

questions.explanation: DISCERN — etymology DIS (apart) + CERNERE (to separate, sift, Latin) = 'to separate apart, distinguish'. Means to perceive, distinguish, especially with EFFORT or with a SHARP, KEEN MIND. SAMPLE USAGES: (1) 'I could barely discern the figure in the fog.' (2) 'It's hard to discern truth from rumor on social media.' (3) 'A wise leader discerns hidden patterns in data.' WORD FAMILY (root CERN/CRET = separate, sift): (1) DISCREET — careful, prudent (separate from indiscretion). (2) DISCRETE — separate, distinct (separate countable units). (3) DISCRIMINATE — to differentiate (positive); also unfair distinction (negative). (4) SECRET — set apart (kept hidden). (5) SECRETE — to hide; also to produce/release (biology). (6) CONCERN (con + cern) — to sift through, care about. (7) CRITERION — standard for judgment (sifting). DON'T CONFUSE: DISCREET (careful) vs DISCRETE (separate). 'A discreet person handles sensitive matters without gossip'; 'discrete data points are individually countable'. SYNONYMS for discern: detect, perceive, distinguish, identify, recognize, notice. ANTONYMS: overlook, miss, ignore. EXAM-FAVORITE pair: DISCREET / DISCRETE distinction in SSC CGL Tier 2, CAT, GRE-tier vocab. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: TELECOMMUTING is a workforce trend where employees:

options.option_text: Work from a distance via technology
Travel to multiple offices daily
Use long phone calls only
Watch television during work hours

questions.explanation: TELECOMMUTING — etymology TELE (far) + COMMUTE (travel to work) = working from FAR/REMOTE location, USING TECHNOLOGY (internet, phone, video conferencing) instead of physically commuting to office. RISE: the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2022) MASSIVELY accelerated telecommuting / 'WORK FROM HOME' (WFH); ~70% of office workers in tech, finance went remote during peak pandemic. Many companies have continued some form of remote/hybrid work. INDIA — IT SECTOR: TCS, Infosys, Wipro had ~3-5% remote pre-pandemic; ~95% during 2020; now ~30-50% hybrid. ADVANTAGES: (1) No commute time/cost (Indian metro commutes can be 2-4 hours daily). (2) Better work-life balance. (3) Wider talent pool (geographic flexibility). (4) Lower office real-estate costs. CHALLENGES: (1) Isolation, mental health. (2) Work-life boundary blurring. (3) Coordination across time zones. (4) Loss of mentorship for juniors. (5) DIGITAL DIVIDE — not all jobs/people can work remotely. RELATED TERMS: TELEWORK, REMOTE WORK, DIGITAL NOMAD, HYBRID WORK. WORLD HUMAN RESOURCES MGMT: 'work from anywhere' policies emerging. PYQ FREQUENCY: telecommuting / WFH in CAT, IBPS PO essay, current affairs.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: TELECAST combines 'tele' (far) with 'cast' (to send out broadly). Which activity does TELECAST most precisely describe?

options.option_text: transmitting a programme to audiences over long distances
projecting moving images onto a large auditorium screen
sending a written message to a recipient in another city
recording a programme for later playback on a local channel

questions.explanation: A is correct because TELECAST = 'cast' (broadcast) + 'tele' (far) — it means transmitting a live or recorded programme to distant viewers via television or radio signals. Option D is the most tempting distractor but recording for local playback involves no long-distance transmission, which is the defining quality of TELECAST.

questions.stem: DISTRIBUTE comes from 'dis-' (apart, in different directions) + 'tribuere' (to assign). Which option BEST captures what the root combination literally suggests?

options.option_text: to carefully collect scattered items into one central location
to divide and spread things out among several recipients
to sort items by category before placing them in storage
to weigh and record items before dispatching them formally

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'dis-' (apart/in different directions) + 'tribuere' (assign) = to assign outward in different directions, i.e., to spread among many recipients. Option A is the near-opposite — it describes gathering, not distributing. Option C (sorting) misses the core idea of spreading outward.

questions.stem: TELEMETRY is critical in space missions and Formula 1 racing. Derived from 'tele' (far) + 'metron' (measure), what is TELEMETRY's primary function?

options.option_text: automatically recording and transmitting data from remote sites
photographing distant objects using powerful zoom lens systems
sending voice commands to remotely operated robotic platforms
navigating between two points using satellite positioning systems

questions.explanation: A is correct: TELEMETRY = measuring ('metron') from far ('tele') — it involves automated sensors that collect data at a remote location and wirelessly transmit it to a base station. Option C (voice commands to robots) describes teleoperation, a common confusion. Option D describes GPS navigation, which is a different technology altogether.

questions.stem: DISTEND (from 'dis-' meaning apart + 'tendere' meaning to stretch) is commonly used in medical descriptions. Which scenario would a physician most accurately describe as DISTENDED?

options.option_text: a joint that has become inflamed and locked in a rigid position
an abdomen that has swollen outward due to trapped gas or fluid
a muscle fibre torn during intense physical training or exercise
a blood vessel that has ruptured under abnormal internal pressure

questions.explanation: B is correct: DISTEND = stretched apart/outward, exactly what happens when the abdomen swells due to trapped gas or ascites. Option D (ruptured vessel) is the most tempting distractor — pressure buildup may precede distension, but rupture is the opposite of stretching; it is tearing apart, described by 'rupture' not 'distend'.

questions.stem: In which of the following words does 'tele-' NOT derive from the Greek root meaning 'far' or 'at a distance', unlike in the remaining three?

options.option_text: TELEPATHY — supposed transmission of thoughts across a distance
TELEMETRY — remote automated measurement sent over a distance
TELEOLOGICAL — concerning ultimate purpose or design in nature
TELECAST — a broadcast transmitted over a long-distance signal

questions.explanation: C is correct: TELEOLOGICAL derives from Greek 'telos' (end, goal, purpose) + 'logos' (study) — it concerns the study of design or purpose in nature (Aristotle's teleology), and has nothing to do with 'tele' meaning far. The other three (TELEPATHY, TELEMETRY, TELECAST) all genuinely use 'tele' = far/at a distance.

questions.stem: DISTRAUGHT is often loosely treated as a synonym for DISTRACTED in everyday speech, but the two differ sharply in degree and etymology. DISTRAUGHT most accurately means:

options.option_text: momentarily startled by an unexpected interruption or loud noise
mildly confused and unable to concentrate on a given task well
persistently worried about minor problems over an extended period
deeply agitated, mentally overwhelmed, and emotionally devastated

questions.explanation: D is correct: DISTRAUGHT (from archaic 'dis-' + 'traught', past participle of 'draw' meaning pulled apart mentally) denotes extreme emotional distress — far beyond mild confusion. Option B (mildly confused) describes DISTRACTED, the most common error. Option C (persistent worry) describes anxiety, which lacks the acute intensity that DISTRAUGHT implies.

questions.stem: DISTASTE, DISTORT, and DISTEND all begin with 'dist-'. However, in DISTASTE specifically, the prefix 'dis-' functions differently from its role in the other two words. In DISTASTE, 'dis-' acts as:

options.option_text: a spatial separator meaning 'apart', as it does in DISTORT fully
a negating or reversing prefix, indicating the absence of taste
an intensifier that sharpens the unpleasantness of a feeling
a directional prefix meaning 'away from', as found in DISTANCE

questions.explanation: B is correct: In DISTASTE, 'dis-' is a negating/reversing prefix (dis + taste = absence of/aversion to taste → strong dislike), the same pattern seen in 'disagree' or 'disapprove'. In contrast, DISTORT (twist apart) and DISTEND (stretch apart) use 'dis-' as a separative prefix meaning 'apart'. Option A is the most tempting error, as candidates often assume all 'dist-' words share the same prefix function.
